summary: Psalm 81 begins as a festival summons: the people are called to sing, play instruments, and blow the trumpet on the appointed feast day. The voice then shifts to God, who recalls rescuing Israel from Egypt, warns against foreign gods, grieves that the people would not listen, and imagines the fullness they could have received.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how Israel's worship joins celebration with memory and warning. In Book III of Psalms, it turns a feast song into a covenant hearing: praise is tied to listening, remembering rescue, and refusing rival gods.

context.author: Associated in the heading with Asaph; Psalms is an anthology with headings whose exact force can include authorship, association, dedication, or collection.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the psalm as Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms may come from different periods, and the final Psalter was shaped over time; Psalm 81 does not identify its date of composition.
context.setting: A public worship setting with song, instruments, trumpet, New Moon, full moon, and feast day language.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and worship song with a preserved heading, a call to praise, and a divine speech recalling the exodus and calling Israel to listen.

outline.heading: Call to festival praise
outline.note: The psalm summons the assembly to sing, shout, bring instruments, and blow the trumpet on the appointed day.

outline.heading: The feast as ordinance
outline.note: The celebration is described as a statute and covenant appointment connected with Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

outline.heading: Rescue remembered
outline.note: God speaks of removing burdens, answering trouble, and testing the people at Meribah.

outline.heading: The central warning
outline.note: God calls Israel to listen, rejects strange and foreign gods, and identifies himself as the one who brought them from Egypt.

outline.heading: Refusal and consequence
outline.note: The people do not listen, so God lets them follow the stubbornness of their own hearts.

outline.heading: The unrealized blessing
outline.note: God longs for Israel to listen and describes what would follow: enemies subdued, lasting punishment for those who hate Yahweh, and wheat and honey for his people.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. On an instrument of Gath. By Asaph. Sing aloud to God, our strength! Make a joyful shout to the God of Jacob!
keyVerses.why: This opening names the psalm's public, musical character and introduces God as Israel's strength.

keyVerses.text: You called in trouble, and I delivered you. I answered you in the secret place of thunder. I tested you at the waters of Meribah.” Selah.
keyVerses.why: The verse holds together rescue and testing, both of which shape the divine speech that follows.

keyVerses.text: I am Yahweh, your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
keyVerses.why: This is the center of the psalm's appeal: the God who rescued Israel calls for exclusive trust and promises provision.

keyVerses.text: Oh that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways!
keyVerses.why: The verse states the longing behind the warning and the promised blessing at the end of the psalm.

themes: no strange god or foreign god
provision imagined as wheat and honey
judgment as being left to stubbornness

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with music and shouting?
questions.answer: The chapter opens as a public call to worship. The people are told to sing, shout, raise a song, bring tambourine, lyre, and harp, and blow the trumpet. The first movement is not private reflection but gathered celebration.

questions.question: What feast day is being described?
questions.answer: The psalm mentions the New Moon, the full moon, and “our feast day,” but it does not name the specific feast. Readers differ on which festival setting best fits the wording. The safest reading from this chapter is that the occasion is an appointed Israelite feast marked by trumpet and music.

questions.question: Who is speaking after verse 5?
questions.answer: The voice shifts into God's first-person speech. God says, “I removed,” “I delivered,” “I answered,” and then addresses Israel directly. The psalm moves from the congregation being summoned to praise into God testifying to the people.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 7 as a preserved performance marker. Its exact instruction is no longer known. Its presence shows that the psalm carries traces of being voiced or performed.

questions.question: Why does God mention Egypt?
questions.answer: Egypt is the memory that grounds the whole appeal. God describes removing a burden, freeing hands from the basket, delivering the people in trouble, and bringing them up out of the land of Egypt. The command not to worship foreign gods is tied to the God who rescued them.

questions.question: What is meant by “strange god” and “foreign god”?
questions.answer: The phrases name rival objects of worship. Verse 9 does not develop a theory of idols; it simply forbids Israel from having a strange god or worshiping any foreign god. In the psalm, that warning stands beside God's claim to be the one who brought Israel from Egypt.

questions.question: Is verse 12 saying God caused the people's stubbornness?
questions.answer: The verse says God “let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts.” It presents judgment as God allowing the people to continue in the counsels they wanted. Readers should be careful not to turn that into a full explanation of divine causation; the chapter's focus is refusal, consequence, and God's desire that they listen.

questions.question: Are verses 14-16 a promise, a memory, or a lament?
questions.answer: They are framed by the longing of verse 13: “Oh that my people would listen to me.” What follows describes what God would do if Israel listened: subdue enemies, confront adversaries, and feed them richly. The grammar makes the ending feel like unrealized blessing rather than a simple report that all this has already happened.

questions.question: What picture does “honey out of the rock” create?
questions.answer: The final line imagines surprising abundance from an unlikely place. Alongside “the finest of the wheat,” it portrays God as able to satisfy the people fully. The psalm does not explain the image mechanically; it uses it poetically to close with provision that Israel has not received because it would not listen.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that marks the psalm for musical or worship use, though the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
A phrase in the heading connected with performance; the chapter preserves it without explaining the instrument’s exact form.
One of the instruments named in the call to praise in verse 2.
The time named in verse 3 for blowing the trumpet, paired there with the full moon and the feast day.
The place-name in verse 7 where God says he tested the people.
The phrase in verse 9 for a rival god Israel is told not to have among them.
